questions.stimulusText:
Mara had crossed the harbor footbridge hundreds of times, but never before sunrise. That morning, fog covered the water so completely that the fishing boats below seemed to have disappeared. She was carrying a repaired brass bell to her grandfather's small ferry, which was scheduled to make its first trip at six.

choices.C: It prevents dust from settling.
choices.D: It causes microorganisms to disappear.

questions.correctAnswer: It protects finer material beneath it from wind erosion.

questions.stimulusText:
Some desert surfaces look as though workers carefully covered them with closely fitted stones. This natural covering is called desert pavement. It can stretch across broad areas, leaving little exposed sand or soil between the rocks.
Scientists once thought wind created these surfaces mainly by blowing away fine particles and leaving larger stones behind. Wind does contribute, but researchers have found that the process can be more complex. In some deserts, dust settles among stones and gradually becomes part of the soil below them. Rainwater carries additional fine material downward. Meanwhile, repeated swelling and shrinking of soil can slowly move stones toward the surface.
The stones themselves also influence what happens next. Once a dense layer forms, it shields much of the finer material underneath from wind erosion. Over long periods, the exposed rocks may develop a dark coating called desert varnish, produced through interactions among minerals, dust, moisture, and microorganisms.
Desert pavement forms slowly, so an undisturbed surface can preserve evidence about environmental conditions over long spans of time. For researchers, these stony landscapes are therefore more than unusual scenery. They can provide clues about how a desert surface has changed.

questions.stimulusText:
When people examine old handwritten books, they often focus first on the main text. Yet historians may be equally interested in marks along the edges of a page. A reader centuries ago might have underlined a sentence, corrected a word, drawn a symbol, or written a short reaction in the margin.
Such notes are called marginalia. They can reveal how people interacted with books rather than merely what books contained. A carefully copied definition may suggest that a reader was studying. An irritated comment beside an argument may reveal disagreement. A pointing hand drawn next to a passage might show that the reader considered those lines especially important.
Marginalia must be interpreted cautiously. A name written inside a book does not prove that the person read every page, and a mysterious mark may have several possible meanings. Researchers compare handwriting, ink, dates, and other evidence before drawing conclusions.
Even with these limits, marginal notes make reading from the past feel unexpectedly active. They remind us that books were not always silent objects resting untouched on shelves. Readers questioned them, learned from them, argued with them, and sometimes left traces of those encounters for someone else to discover centuries later.

questions.stimulusText:
Noah had planned to spend Saturday morning testing the kite he had built from thin wooden strips and bright paper. By breakfast, however, the sky was completely still. The leaves on the maple tree outside barely moved.
His younger cousin Elise studied the kite leaning against the porch wall. “Maybe it needs something else,” she said.
“It needs wind,” Noah replied.
Instead of waiting, Elise carried several scraps of ribbon to the table and began tying them to a short piece of string. Noah watched as she tested different lengths by pulling the string through the air. One ribbon fluttered freely while another twisted around itself.
Soon Noah joined her. They shortened the tail of the kite, changed the spacing between the ribbons, and reinforced one corner that had begun to bend. They could not test whether the kite would fly, but they could improve parts of its design.
By late afternoon, a breeze finally stirred the branches. Noah ran across the field while Elise held the kite above her head. When she released it, the kite climbed steadily instead of spinning as it had during earlier trials that week.
Noah laughed. The wind had arrived, but he realized the quiet morning had not been wasted after all.

questions.stimulusTitle: Reading a Building Through Its Repairs
questions.stimulusText:
Old buildings are often described by the year they were constructed, but that single date can hide a much longer story. Over decades or centuries, owners repair roofs, replace windows, close doorways, add rooms, and adapt interiors to new uses. Architectural historians study these changes because alterations can reveal how people lived and what they valued.
Evidence may appear in unexpected places. A patch of differently colored brick can indicate where a doorway once stood. Marks in wooden beams may show that a wall or staircase was moved. Layers of paint can reveal changing preferences, while nail holes or grooves may suggest the former location of shelves, signs, or partitions.
Researchers do not assume that every unusual feature has an important explanation. Materials may have been reused simply because they were available, and repairs sometimes resulted from ordinary damage rather than major changes in a building's purpose. For that reason, physical evidence is often compared with maps, photographs, receipts, or written records.
Studying repairs transforms a building from a fixed object into a record of decisions. A structure may begin as a home, later become a shop, and eventually serve as an office. The walls remain, but the evidence within them can reveal a sequence of human choices.

Nia found the map folded inside a field notebook her aunt had left on the kitchen table. “Why not make it permanent?” Nia asked.
“Because a useful map sometimes needs to admit what may change,” her aunt replied.

questions.stimulusText:
Elias had agreed to operate the lights for a neighborhood theater production because he preferred working where the audience could not see him. During rehearsals, he sat at a small control board, following numbered cues written beside the script.
Two days before opening night, the actor playing the messenger lost his voice. The director scanned the room and asked Elias to read the messenger’s six lines during rehearsal so the other actors could continue practicing.
Elias resisted at first. He knew every lighting cue but had never spoken from the stage. Finally, he carried the script to the empty set. His first line came out so quietly that the director asked him to repeat it.

questions.stimulusTitle: How Tree Rings Record More Than Age
questions.stimulusText:
Each year, many trees growing in seasonal climates add a new layer of wood beneath their bark. When a trunk is viewed in cross section, these layers often appear as rings. Counting the rings can provide an estimate of a tree’s age, but researchers can learn much more from them.
The width of a ring reflects conditions that affected growth during a particular season. In some environments, plentiful moisture and favorable temperatures may produce wider rings, while drought can contribute to narrower ones. However, ring width cannot be interpreted by a single rule everywhere. Different tree species respond differently, and factors such as crowding, disease, or damage can also influence growth.
Researchers therefore compare patterns across many trees from the same region. If numerous trees show unusually narrow growth during the same period, a shared environmental cause becomes more likely. Scientists can also match overlapping ring patterns from living trees and older wood. This method can extend a regional record farther into the past than the lifespan of any one tree.
Tree-ring evidence is especially useful when combined with other records, such as historical observations or measurements from sediments. Rather than acting as a perfect diary, tree rings provide clues. Their value comes from careful comparison, context, and the recognition that several factors can leave similar marks.

questions.stimulusText:
In the early years of public bicycle manufacturing, inventors often received attention for dramatic new designs. Yet many practical advances came from less celebrated workers who improved ordinary parts. One such fictionalized example is Clara Venn, a skilled machinist working in a small industrial shop at the turn of the twentieth century.
Venn’s daily work involved shaping metal fittings used on several kinds of machines. When a local bicycle maker began ordering parts from the shop, she noticed that mechanics repeatedly filed the same bracket by hand before installation. The bracket worked, but its original shape made assembly unnecessarily slow.
Rather than proposing an entirely new bicycle, Venn changed the angle and placement of two holes in the bracket. She produced several samples, asked mechanics to test them, and adjusted the design after hearing their comments. The final version could be installed more quickly with fewer corrections.
The improvement was modest, and customers buying bicycles probably never knew about it. For the workshop, however, the change reduced wasted effort and made production more consistent.
Stories like Venn’s illustrate an important feature of technological development. Progress is not always a sequence of famous inventions. It can also grow through careful observation, repeated testing, and small changes made by people close to the work itself.

Yet many practical advances came from less celebrated workers who improved ordinary parts. One such fictionalized example is Clara Venn, a skilled machinist working in a small industrial shop at the turn of the twentieth century.
Venn’s daily work involved shaping metal fittings used on several kinds of machines. When a local bicycle maker began ordering parts from the shop, she noticed that mechanics repeatedly filed the same bracket by hand before installation. The bracket worked, but its original shape made assembly unnecessarily slow.
Rather than proposing an entirely new bicycle, Venn changed the angle and placement of two holes in the bracket. She produced several samples, asked mechanics to test them, and adjusted the design after hearing their comments. The final version could be installed more quickly with fewer corrections.
The improvement was modest, and customers buying bicycles probably never knew about it. For the workshop, however, the change reduced wasted effort and made production more consistent.
Stories like Venn’s illustrate an important feature of technological development. Progress is not always a sequence of famous inventions. It can also grow through careful observation, repeated testing, and small changes made by people close to the work itself.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of the passage?

choices.A: To argue that famous inventions rarely work
choices.B: To explain why bicycles were difficult to manufacture
choices.C: To compare several competing bicycle companies
choices.D: To show how small, practical improvements can contribute to technological progress

questions.correctAnswer: To show how small, practical improvements can contribute to technological progress
questions.explanation: The final paragraph explicitly broadens Venn's modest improvement into a point about how progress can occur.
